title: ABCD SYNDROME
alt_titles: ALBINISM, BLACK LOCK, CELL MIGRATION DISORDER OF THE NEUROCYTES OF THE GUT, AND DEAFNESS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ABCD syndrome (ABCDS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.

checks.claim: ABCD syndrome is caused by homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.
checks.evidence_quote: ABCD syndrome is caused by a homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.

paragraphs.text: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive neural crest disorder characterized by albinism, a black lock of hair, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut (Hirschsprung disease), and deafness (Gross et al., 1995; Verheij et al., 2002). Verheij et al. (2002) noted that the phenotype overlaps with Shah-Waardenburg syndrome and suggested that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Gross et al. (1995) reported a macrosomic newborn girl, the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents, with albinism, a black lock at the right temporo-occipital region, and retinal depigmentation. Bilateral deafness was confirmed by brainstem auditory-evoked potentials. She also had a severe defect of intestinal innervation: biopsy showed aganglionosis of the large intestine and total absence of neurocytes and nerve fibers in the small intestine, indicating a total lack of sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation. The infant died of intestinal dysfunction at 5 weeks. Four sibs had the same syndrome and died a few days after birth; the other 9 sibs were well, with an unremarkable phenotype. Gross et al. (1995) considered the disorder to be a new neural crest syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Because the ABCD syndrome phenotype overlaps with Shah-Waardenburg syndrome (sensorineural deafness; hypopigmentation of skin, hair, and irides; and Hirschsprung disease), Verheij et al. (2002) screened DNA of the index patient of the family reported by Gross et al. (1995) for mutations in the endothelin B receptor gene (EDNRB), which is known to be involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome. They identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene. Verheij et al. (2002) suggested that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.

clinical_synopsis.feature: Aganglionosis of the large intestine (Hirschsprung disease)
Total absence of neurocytes and nerve fibers in the small intestine
Death in infancy from intestinal dysfunction
Black lock of hair (right temporo-occipital region)

paragraphs.text: In the index patient of the consanguineous Kurdish family with ABCD syndrome reported by Gross et al. (1995), Verheij et al. (2002) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 of the EDNRB gene, resulting in an arg201-to-ter (R201X) substitution. The mutation was found by screening the EDNRB gene because of the phenotypic overlap with Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.
